findings.reader_payoff: The opening journey sits at the head of a passage about receiving and bearing guidance, so its signs begin a history of response rather than remaining an isolated spectacle.
findings.containment: The traveler is not identified with Moses or the descendants, and the focus does not explicitly commission him to transmit a Book. The HFT's alternative remains live: these may be adjacent examples of divine favor rather than one custodial chain.

epistemic.reason: The focus QAC and supplied context root occurrences verify every cited HFT coordinate and root; the HFT reader identity is legacy_unbound, so the sequence and custodianship relation remain attributed.

findings.containment: The focus's divine signs and the record of deeds are different kinds of evidence; the packet does not equate them or identify the Book in 17:2 with the personal record. The HFT's alternative that these are separate evidentiary settings remains live.

epistemic.reason: The Arabic and context root occurrences verify the HFT's 17:13-15 coordinates; the continuum from revelation to self-witness is an attributed inference from a legacy_unbound source.

findings.title: The Servant Seen in Return
findings.claim: The focus shows signs to a servant and ends with the all-seeing; 17:17 speaks of servants whose sins are known by an expert and seen. The pericope turns the focus's one-way disclosure toward a reciprocal relation in which the recipient also remains visible and answerable.
findings.mechanism: The focus's servant, showing, and sight meet the later servants, their culpable acts, inward knowledge, and the repeated seeing word. That return changes the focal privilege of seeing into a relation that also exposes the observer.
findings.reader_payoff: The servant who sees signs remains within the sight and knowledge that the focus names at its close.
findings.containment: The later formula may simply affirm divine omniscience without directly revising the journey. The reciprocal gaze is a contextual inference, not a claim that the focus encounter causes the later judgment across generations.

epistemic.reason: All focus and 17:17 root/index coordinates match the supplied Arabic and focus QAC; the reciprocal relation remains an inference attributed to a legacy_unbound HFT source.

findings.title: Servanthood as Supported Motion
findings.claim: The focus says God carries His servant by night to show him signs. In 17:20 both groups receive extension and gift, while 17:22 warns that rival worship leaves a person sitting, blamed, and forsaken. Read together, dependence is the relation that carries motion and support, while divided dependence ends in isolation.
findings.mechanism: The focus's conducted travel and servant meet unbarred giving in 17:20 and the contrast between exclusive worship, sitting, and abandonment in 17:22. This contact recasts servanthood from passive subordination as a relation in which motion and perception are enabled by another's support.
findings.reader_payoff: The servant's dependence can be seen alongside honor, movement, and received provision; its counterpart in the same passage is unsupported immobility.
findings.containment: 17:20 says that both groups receive from the Lord's gift; it does not say those gifts cause the focus journey. 17:22 has its own warning about rival worship, and the movement/sitting contrast is an attributed inference that may be a juxtaposition.

epistemic.reason: Every HFT source coordinate matches the supplied focus QAC or context root occurrence; the support-versus-immobility synthesis remains attributed to a legacy_unbound source and retains its stated alternative.

findings.title: The Singular Servant in a Collective Prayer
findings.claim: The focus names one servant carried to see signs; external 1:5 answers with a plural voice: "we worship You and we seek Your help." The direct servant-word contact adds a communal devotional perspective to the singular narrative recipient.
findings.mechanism: The focus's عَبْدِ shares its root with نَعْبُدُ in 1:5, and the same plural utterance pairs worship with seeking aid. The contact shifts the reader's stance from observing one recipient of divine action to hearing a community voice its own dependence.
findings.reader_payoff: The focus's servant relation can be held beside a first-person plural act of worship and request for aid, bringing the singular event into a communal devotional frame.
findings.containment: This overlay does not identify the traveler with Fatiha's speakers or say that the journey answers their prayer. Native 17:22 already states exclusive worship; the external addition contributes the collective pronoun and explicit request for aid, while the connection itself remains exploratory.

epistemic.reason: The focus and 1:5 surfaces supply a direct root echo and plural grammar; relating the narrated servant to a communal prayer is an authorial overlay, and the prayer may remain a separate utterance.
